---
title: "03 — Fabry–Pérot cavity"
---

Different physics: an optical cavity is a single-pole low-pass,

$$G(s) = \frac{\omega_c}{s + \omega_c}$$

with the cavity pole `fc` setting the bandwidth.
There is no sharp resonance to aim at; the identification is signal-to-noise
limited — the parameter of interest (`fc`) affects the shape of `|G(f)|`
near the pole, which here sits at 100 Hz.

This example shows the estimator recovering the cavity pole from a noisy
measurement with a 30% wrong prior.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

from system_ident.model import TFModel
from system_ident.estimators.invfreqs import InvfreqsEstimator

fc = 100.0                              # true cavity pole [Hz]
wc = 2 * np.pi * fc
true  = TFModel.from_zpk(zeros=[], poles=[-wc], gain=wc)    # DC gain = 1

freq = np.logspace(0, 3, 400)          # 1 Hz … 1 kHz (log-spaced)
H    = true.eval(freq)
```

## Measurement and fit

```{python}
rng   = np.random.default_rng(0)
H_err = np.abs(H) * 0.05               # 5% noise
H_meas = H + (rng.standard_normal(freq.size) + 1j * rng.standard_normal(freq.size)) * H_err / np.sqrt(2)

# Prior: 30% off on the pole location
prior = TFModel.from_zpk(zeros=[], poles=[-2*np.pi*70.0], gain=2*np.pi*70.0)
fit   = InvfreqsEstimator().fit(freq, H_meas, H_err, prior)

# Extract the fitted pole frequency
f_pole_fit   = abs(fit.den[1]) / (2 * np.pi)
f_pole_prior = abs(prior.den[1]) / (2 * np.pi)
print(f"Prior cavity pole:  {f_pole_prior:.1f} Hz  (30% wrong)")
print(f"True  cavity pole:  {fc:.1f} Hz")
print(f"Fit   cavity pole:  {f_pole_fit:.2f} Hz  (error: {abs(f_pole_fit-fc)/fc*100:.2f}%)")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-cavity
#| fig-cap: "Single-pole cavity: noisy measurement and recovered fit. Use the log x-axis to see the pole region near 100 Hz. The prior (70 Hz) is shown in red; the fit converges to the true 100 Hz pole."

SKY  = '#1F8AC0'
GOLD = '#C8973A'
RED  = '#E53E3E'
GRAY = '#94A3B8'

fig = go.Figure()

fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=freq, y=np.abs(H), mode='lines',
    line=dict(color=SKY, width=2.5), name=f'True plant  (f_c = {fc:.0f} Hz)',
    hovertemplate='%{x:.2f} Hz   |G| = %{y:.5f}<extra></extra>',
))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=freq, y=np.abs(H_meas), mode='markers',
    marker=dict(color='rgba(148,163,184,0.45)', size=3), name='Measured (5% noise)',
    hovertemplate='%{x:.2f} Hz   |Hmeas| = %{y:.5f}<extra></extra>',
))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=freq, y=np.abs(prior.eval(freq)), mode='lines',
    line=dict(color=RED, width=1.8, dash='dot'),
    name=f'Prior  (f_c = {f_pole_prior:.0f} Hz)',
    hovertemplate='%{x:.2f} Hz   |G_prior| = %{y:.5f}<extra></extra>',
))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=freq, y=np.abs(fit.eval(freq)), mode='lines',
    line=dict(color=GOLD, width=2.2, dash='dash'),
    name=f'Fitted  (f_c = {f_pole_fit:.1f} Hz)',
    hovertemplate='%{x:.2f} Hz   |G_fit| = %{y:.5f}<extra></extra>',
))

# Annotate the true pole
fig.add_vline(
    x=fc, line_color='rgba(31,138,192,0.35)', line_dash='dot', line_width=1.5,
)
fig.add_annotation(
    x=np.log10(fc), y=0.0, xref='x', yref='paper',
    text=f'<b>f_c = {fc:.0f} Hz</b>',
    showarrow=False, xanchor='left', yanchor='bottom',
    font=dict(size=11, color=SKY, family='Outfit, sans-serif'),
    xshift=8, yshift=6,
)

fig.update_layout(
    template='plotly_white', height=400,
    margin=dict(l=60, r=20, t=20, b=55),
    font=dict(family='Outfit, Inter, sans-serif', size=12),
    legend=dict(orientation='h', yanchor='bottom', y=1.02, xanchor='right', x=1,
                bgcolor='rgba(255,255,255,0.9)', bordercolor='#DCE5F0', borderwidth=1),
    xaxis=dict(title='Frequency  [Hz]', type='log', gridcolor='rgba(30,60,100,0.07)'),
    yaxis=dict(title='|G(f)|', type='log', gridcolor='rgba(30,60,100,0.07)'),
)
fig.show()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Log-spaced frequency grid

For a single-pole system, the pole region spans roughly a decade around `fc`.
Using a log-spaced frequency grid (as here) samples this region well; a
linear grid would waste most of its points on frequencies far from the pole.
The `InvfreqsEstimator` naturally handles non-uniform frequency grids since
it weights each bin by the measurement variance.
:::
